claims.text: The starting W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf alloy is a homogenized, single-phase tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with minimal precipitation.
Controlled aging between 700°C and 900°C will produce stepwise coherent nanoprecipitates in W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf.
Aging can be tailored to generate fine coherent precipitates while avoiding undesirable intermetallic formation.
Performing the aging treatment in an inert atmosphere will avoid oxidation.
The proposed treatment will create a uniform dispersion of fine coherent nanoprecipitates throughout the matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitates will act as efficient sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
The nanoprecipitates will trap vacancies and interstitials and promote their recombination.
Enhanced point-defect recombination will suppress the formation and growth of voids and other irradiation-induced defect clusters.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations associated with premature crack initiation.
Coherent nanoprecipitation can provide high strength together with substantial tensile ductility in a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
Under heavy-ion or neutron irradiation near 800°C, the aged alloy will exhibit less void swelling than the unaged alloy.
Under irradiation near 800°C, the aged alloy will exhibit a lower defect density than the unaged alloy.
Under irradiation near 800°C, the aged alloy will maintain or improve yield strength and ductility relative to the unaged alloy.
The unaged tungsten-based alloy typically develops greater swelling and more extensive defect clustering under irradiation.
Radiation-tolerance and mechanical-property benefits depend on attaining an optimal precipitate size and distribution.
Precipitate coarsening or an inhomogeneous precipitate distribution may cause mechanical embrittlement.
The aging parameters needed to reproducibly obtain the proposed optimal precipitate structure are not yet established.
